Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Oregon statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Oregon property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Petitions to the county property value appeals board are filed with the board clerk after tax statements are mailed and by December 31. (ORS 309.100(2); source)
  • The board may convene on or after the first Monday in February and must adjourn no later than April 15. (ORS 309.026; source)
  • The board hears petitions to reduce real market value, assessed value, or maximum assessed value as of January 1. (ORS 309.026(2); source)
  • If a taxpayer may appeal to the property value appeals board, no Tax Court appeal is allowed until the board order issues; Tax Court appeal is from the board order. (ORS 305.275(3); source)
  • An appeal to the Tax Court from a county property value appeals board order must be filed within 30 days of the order mailing, publication or delivery date. (ORS 305.280(4); source)
  • Real and personal property is valued at 100 percent of real market value; assessed value is generally the lesser of maximum assessed value or real market value. (ORS 308.232; 308.146; source)
  • Maximum assessed value equals 103 percent of prior-year assessed value or 100 percent of prior-year maximum assessed value, whichever is greater. (ORS 308.146(1); source)
  • A person aggrieved by an omitted-property assessment may appeal to the Tax Court within 90 days after the roll correction. (ORS 311.223(4); source)
  • Real property is subject to tax foreclosure when three years have elapsed from the earliest delinquency. (ORS 312.010(1); source)
  • The county holds foreclosed property for two years from the judgment date unless redeemed. (ORS 312.120(1); source)

How to sell a Oregon house when this applies to you

  1. Find out what the title and escrow company needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.
  4. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. We buy houses as-is, with no repairs and no agent commission. See we buy houses in Oregon.

What a cash sale of a Oregon house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Oregon.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Oregon disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Oregon

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Oregon change, so confirm details with the official office or a Oregon attorney or tax professional.

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Oregon offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules. Here is what the official sources say.

  • Oregon's statutory homestead exemption protects a homestead from execution, judgment liens and debts up to $150,000 (combined $300,000 for two or more household judgment debtors), indexed annually. (ORS 18.395(1)(a),(d); source)
  • For child support, spousal support or restitution judgments the homestead exemption is $40,000 ($50,000 combined). (ORS 18.395(1)(b); source)
  • The homestead must be the actual abode of and occupied by the owner or the owner's spouse, parent or child. (ORS 18.395(1)(c); source)
  • The exemption is effective without a claim by the judgment debtor and extends to sale proceeds held up to one year with intent to buy another homestead. (ORS 18.395(1)(a),(2); source)
  • The exemption applies to a manufactured dwelling, floating home, and a purchaser's interest under a land sale contract. (ORS 18.395(9),(10); source)
  • Separate from the creditor exemption, Oregon offers property tax deferral on an owner-occupied homestead for qualifying seniors/persons with a disability (ORS 311.666 to 311.701). (ORS 311.666; source)

Oregon Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Oregon
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • Zero fees, zero commissions, zero closing costs
  • No obligation: turn the offer down and owe us nothing

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Oregon statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Oregon evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment: 10 days' written notice (not before the 8th day of the rental period) or 13 days' notice (not before the 5th day) for non-weekly tenancies. (ORS 90.394(2); source)
  • Week-to-week nonpayment notice is 72 hours, given no sooner than the fifth day. (ORS 90.394(1); source)
  • For-cause notices must give at least 30 days to terminate, with a cure date at least 14 days after delivery if curable. (ORS 90.392(3),(4); source)
  • After judgment of restitution, the clerk issues a notice of restitution giving at least four days to move out, then a writ of execution is served by the sheriff. (ORS 105.151; source)
  • An unenforced writ expires after 30 days. (ORS 105.161(3); source)
  • The landlord's possession action is brought in circuit court or justice court in the county where the premises sit. (ORS 105.110; source)
  • After the first year, a landlord may end a month-to-month tenancy for a qualifying reason, including accepting a purchase offer from a buyer who will occupy as primary residence. (ORS 90.427(3)(c),(5)(a)(D); source)
  • Such notice is 90 days, or 60 days if the landlord pays one month's rent in addition and provides written evidence of the offer. (ORS 90.427(5)(a),(b); source)
  • A landlord ending a tenancy under subsection (5) must state the reason and pay one month's rent, except landlords owning four or fewer units. (ORS 90.427(6); source)
  • Terminating in violation makes the landlord liable for three months' rent plus actual damages. (ORS 90.427(9); source)
  • If the dwelling shares a property with the landlord's residence (two units or fewer), 30 days' notice applies when a buyer will occupy. (ORS 90.427(8)(a)(C); source)
  • In foreclosure sales, bona fide tenants get at least 30 days (month-to-month) or 60 days (fixed term) after written termination notice. (ORS 86.771(10); source)

This guide covers Oregon foreclosure sales according to official sources. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • A judgment debtor may redeem property sold at an execution sale within 180 days after the sale date. (ORS 18.964(1); source)
  • A lien claimant may redeem within 60 days after the sale date. (ORS 18.964(2); source)
  • A judgment creditor may bid orally or submit a written bid at least 48 hours before the sale, not exceeding the judgment amount plus recoverable sale costs. (ORS 18.936; source)
  • The sheriff delivers net sale proceeds to the court administrator, and the court enters an order of distribution. (ORS 18.950(1); source)
  • If a homestead exemption applies, the sheriff may not sell unless the bid exceeds sale costs plus the exemption amount. (ORS 18.395(8); source)
  • A homestead occupied by the debtor may not be sold on execution to satisfy a judgment of $3,000 or less at entry. (ORS 18.395(5); source)
  • Notice of sale must be served or mailed at least 120 days before the trustee's sale, after the notice of default is recorded. (ORS 86.764(1); source)
  • Notice of sale must go to the grantor, successors in interest of record, and subsequent lienholders of record. (ORS 86.764(2); source)
  • The default may be cured up to five days before the last-set sale date by paying the amount due plus costs and fees ($1,000 combined trustee and attorney fees for residential trust deeds, or actual if less). (ORS 86.778(1); source)
  • A trustee's sale forecloses and terminates interests of noticed persons, who may not redeem from the purchaser. (ORS 86.797(1); source)
  • No deficiency action may follow a trustee's sale or judicial foreclosure of a residential trust deed. (ORS 86.797(2); source)
  • Judicial foreclosure of a lien is by suit; a complaint on a residential trust deed must attach resolution-conference compliance documents. (ORS 88.010; source)
  • A judgment of foreclosure orders the property sold; judicial-sale redemption follows execution-sale rules (ORS 18.860 to 18.993). (ORS 88.106; source)

  • Claims not listed may be barred unless presented within four months of the affidavit filing or a personal representative petition is filed. (ORS 114.525(1)(v); source)
  • After the four-month claim period (absent a personal representative petition) the affiant transfers remaining property; real property transfer requires recording. (ORS 114.555; source)
  • The affidavit must describe estate property, including a legal description of any real property, and list heirs, devisees and creditors. (ORS 114.525(1); source)
  • Sales by court-appointed personal representatives are excluded from the seller's property disclosure statement requirement. (ORS 105.470(3); source)

What a cash sale of a Oregon house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Oregon.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.

  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Oregon disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Oregon

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Oregon change, so confirm details with the official office or a Oregon attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Oregon

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Who can sell a house in probate?

The personal representative with court authority signs for the estate.
